content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper theoretically analyzes the subnetwork performance with respect to the number of SGD pre-training iterations based on greedy forward selection (Ye2020). The discovered findings make a good connection with the existing empirical study, such as early-bird tickets.
content.main_review:
##########################################################################

Pros: 

 

1. The paper is well written and easy to follow. Assumption 1 is quite common in practice, i.e., Relu. 

 
2. The theoretical insights provided by the paper are in line with the empirical findings in the existing works.

3. The findings in Figure2 are quite interesting.


##########################################################################

Cons: 

1. I expect that there are some terms in the bound that can represent the sparsity of the subnetworks, since the sparsity of the subnetwork is highly correlated with the performance.  However, I am somehow missing this in the bound. Can the authors please clarify this?

2. It is not clear to me that the experimental results are averaged with multiple runs or just once. As shown in Table 1, the difference between some settings is very small. It is not clear to me if this accuracy difference is caused by randomness or the theoretical bound provided. 

3. It is unclear to me why this paper focuses on "greedy forward selection'' for pruning. Methods like iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) are more commonly used in practice. Theoretical study on IMP is definitely more valuable for the community.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work aims to analyze the correlation between the pre-training time of the dense network and the performance of the subnetwork. Although the study on this problem is important and the bound seems to be correct, the story and experimental results need a bit more work.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1242 by Reviewer 5KAU

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5KAU
content.comment:
We respond to each of the points below, though we would like to emphasize that the few, minor comments presented in the review are not reflective of the low score given to our paper. The authors would greatly appreciate more explanation/understanding as to why our paper was rated poorly.

1. Yes, the sparsity of the network is given by $k$. This can be seen in Lemma 1. However, after Lemma 1, we study the amount of dense network pre-training iterations that would eliminate the factor of $k$ in the numerator of (11). We show within the proof of Theorem 1 (appendix A.2.1) that the only way to eliminate this factor is to increase SGD training iterations (i.e., this factor cannot be eliminated via some pruning constant). Thus, $k$ is not present in the bound for Theorem 1. Generally, $k$ does not show up in theorem 1 because we are simply demonstrating how much pre-training is needed such that we achieve a $O(1/k)$ rate of decay in pruning error (i.e., this implies that pruned networks of increasing sizes will have lower and lower loss). The value of $k$ will then indeed impact the final performance once pruning is performed, but it is not present in analyzing the amount of SGD training needed for pruning to work well. 

2. For MLP experiments and CIFAR10, we run 3 trials and take an average. For ImageNet, we run single trials due to the computational expense. We would  be glad to clarify this in the writing. 

3. We focus on greedy forward selection because the update rule (which is similar to Frank-Wolfe) is particularly suited for enabling the analysis we provide -- from a theoretical perspective the behavior/structure of this algorithm allows a lot of interesting analysis to be performed, where our work is a single example. Although we agree studying IMP would be useful, it is unclear whether deriving such a result would even be possible from a theoretical perspective --- greedy forward selection is designed in a way that makes it apt to theoretical analysis, and a lot of analytical tools from the convergence analysis of Frank-Wolfe-style algorithms can be leveraged. We emphasize that $i)$ oftentimes the SOTA empirical approaches in deep learning are not amenable to theoretical analysis, leading researchers to find simplified cases where theoretical analysis is possible (e.g., neural network analysis based on shallow networks, gaussian input data assumptions, infinite network width, etc.), $ii)$ deriving these results for greedy forward selection (which has been utilized in top-conference papers [1, 2]!) was highly non-trivial, and $iii)$ greedy forward selection (although not as popular as IMP) is still a valid pruning algorithm that has been shown to yield good (possibly even superior) pruning results in large-scale experimentation.

References:

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.01794 

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.15969

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper conducts a theoretical analysis on the relationship between training sample number and pre-training iteration number for network pruning. The result shows that for the two-layer network pruning problem, the SGD pre-training iteration number is logarithmically dependent on the training sample number.
content.main_review:
In Theorem 1, there is an assumption that Nd > m^2, which is hard to be satisfied in real network training problems. Considering the major result of Theorem 2 is highly correlated with Theorem 1, it is questionable that the established analysis is effective.

The experiment result cannot well support the established theoretical analysis. The logarithmically dependent on the training sample number cannot be observed from Figure 2. The experiment results on deeper networks conclude that training a larger model needs more iterations. This is an obvious intuition, which is too weak without sufficient detail to support the theoretical result.
content.summary_of_the_review: My major concern includes (1) over-ideal assumptions in the Theorems and (2) the experiment lacks sufficient details to support the main theoretical results.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1242 by Reviewer 888m

content.title: Response to Reviewer 888m
content.comment:
"$\textit{In Theorem 1, there … effective}$"

Note that the overparameterization assumption of $Nd > m^2$ is state-of-the-art in theoretical analysis to the best of our knowledge. Only recently (and after the submission of this work) it was proved that the overparameterization assumption could be subquadratic [2]; but again, our theory could be amenable to adapt to that theory also. The overparameterization assumption we use in this work is significantly more mild than a large number of papers that come before it. See Appendix A.2 for more in-depth discussion and references to numerous previous papers that rely upon significantly increased overparameterization requirements. 

Generally, we emphasize that the $Nd > m^2$ requirement, presented in [1], is provided within a paper titled “towards moderate overparameterization”. In other words, the entire purpose of that paper was providing convergence guarantees with more realistic overparameterization requirements. Thus, criticizing our paper for using this assumption is somewhat peculiar --- we find this main criticism to our paper invalid to justify the low score we got.

"$\textit{The experiment result cannot … Figure 2.}$"

We would appreciate details on how Figure 2 does not demonstrate a logarithmic dependence. We linearly vary the size of the datasets, and the amount of required pre-training to discover a good sub network reaches a clear plateau. Although one could argue this is not exactly logarithmic, we are not sure what more can be done in a practical experiment.  

"$\textit{The experiment results on … the theoretical result.}$”

This is simply incorrect. Our experiments on deeper networks conclude that fewer pre-training iterations are needed to discover a high-performing subnetwork on smaller datasets, not that “training a larger model needs more iterations”.  In fact, we explicitly discuss the fact that pre-training requirements not being asymptotically dependent on model size is interesting.

We emphasize that creating a model that contains good subnetworks is not as simple as training the model to reach a good accuracy -- good subnetworks may exist within randomly initialized models or models that are minimally trained. In other words, although subnetworks will likely exist if a network is trained for a long time and performs well, they generally exist long before this.  Our work analyzes the point in training at which these subnetworks are guaranteed to be present. Within the literature, the properties that cause good subnetworks to arise during training are not clearly known. As such, summarizing our analysis as showing "training a larger model needs more iterations" is oversimplified and misleading.

References:

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04674

[2] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.01875.pdf

display_title: Official Review of Paper1242 by Reviewer Sdn8

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper study the minimum number of pre-training iterations to make pruning successful. A theoretical justification is provided based on the analysis for a two-layer network. The authors empirically verify their theoretical findings on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet with MobileNet and ResNet.
content.main_review:
* In Figure 2, 'thousands' --> '1x10^3'
* In Figure 2, the accuracy is visualized by the color of each cell. Since accuracy is one of the most important metrics, it should be visualized with lines. 
* A conclusion reached by this paper is 'number of pretraining iterations depends on dataset size instead of model size.' However, when dataset size changed, it is more appropriate to measure number of epochs instead of iterations.  During training, with the same batch size, if the dataset size is smaller, one should be able to achieve the accuracy saturation with fewer iteration. So, ''smaller dataset ---> fewer iteration'' is somehow trivial. 
* Another interesting and **related** question is how large dataset we should use. According to the authors' conclusion, you can do fewer pre-training iterations to find the sparse net for a smaller dataset. From a different perspective, suppose we do enough pre-training iterations, what is the best pruning accuracy we are able to achieve with a smaller dataset, is this accuracy is much lower than using the full-dataset. If so, fewer pre-training iterations is a result of lower performance in purpose. 
* Figure 2 is crucial to understand the proposed method. Instead of using three sub-plots, the author can make a plot, where x-axis is the size of model and the y-axis pruned accuracy given a fixed number of pre-training iterations.  
* In table 2, the most aggressive pruning ratio is ~(100-65). I am interested in seeing whether the conclusion is more pronounced for more aggressive pruning.
content.summary_of_the_review: The discussed problem is important and interesting. Some presentation and analysis need to be further improved.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Sdn8
content.comment:
We answer the questions raised below. Yet, we kindly request that the reviewer better explain the reasoning for the low score on our paper, given that most of the comments refer to personal taste and are not constructive comments on ideas included in the paper. 

1. Sure, we can fix this.

2. There are three important metrics, as we are considering how accuracy changes with respect to dataset size and pre-training amount. We try to make fixed accuracy levels clear by adding the red line to visualize the amount of pre-training needed to reach fixed accuracy levels. We could consider making some kind of 3D plot to make this more clear if it is a significant issue.

3. We consider iterations because dataset sizes vary across different experiments. Comparing in terms of epochs would be unfair because models trained on larger datasets would receive more supervision and take longer to train per epoch. Generally, we disagree that considering epochs is more appropriate. While the conclusion that “smaller dataset → fewer iterations” is trivial, the actual conclusion we make (i.e., that smaller datasets require fewer iterations of pre-training to discover a subnetwork that matches the final/fully-trained network performance) is not. Namely, the reviewer mistakes the idea of training a network to perform well with obtaining a network that contains good subnetworks -- good subnetworks may exist in a network that is fully trained, partially trained, or even not trained at all. As such, the factors that cause good subnetworks to arise in different experimental settings is not clearly known or trivial, and the conclusion outlined by the reviewer (i.e., "smaller dataset ---> fewer iteration") is a drastic oversimplification/misunderstanding of the findings of the paper.

4. We agree this is an interesting related question for future work. 

5. Yes. We can modify figure 2 based on your suggestions and agree it can be improved. 

6. This pruning ratio is pretty aggressive in comparison to previous work (i.e., probably pruning more than this would begin to significantly deteriorate performance); see for example the tables for the same models in [1, 2]. 

References:

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.01794 

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.15969

display_title: Official Review of Paper1242 by Reviewer Fxr2

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose an analysis on the neural networks pruning technique, and in particular, they theoretically prove that there exists a bound in the number of SGD pre-training iterations beyond which pruning via greedy forward selection yields a subnetwork that achieves good training error. The theoretical discussion is limited to a very specific model (a two-layer, fully-connected network), while the empirical evaluation involves also other architectures.
content.main_review:
Even if the proposed theoretical analysis is interesting in my opinion, the novelty proposed by the authors in this manuscript is below the average for an ICLR paper, in particular, because the authors do not propose a novel solution based on the theoretical observation that they proposed. Moreover, the most interesting part of the analysis is limited to a very specific model. In general, the paper is well written and pleasant to read, but at some points, the discussion should be extended and clarified.

In section 2 the discussed 2 layers network (eq (1)) has a very particular architecture since it presents a single layer of neurons whose outputs are summed and divided by the number of neurons.  It seems more similar to a single layer model since no linear transformation that involves trainable parameters is applied on the output of the first layer of neurons. Please clarify which parameters are exploited by each layer of the architecture.

For what concerns the structure of the paper, in my opinion,  section 5 ("Related Work") should be moved in before section two. Moreover, section 5 should be extended explaining in more detail some of the considered work, in particular (Ye et al., 2020) and  (Oymak & Soltanolkotabi, 2019) that are useful to understand the proof of Lemma 1 and how Theorem 1 has been derived.

The authors state that the number of SGD iterations above which a pruned subnet achieves a good training loss is dependent on the size of the dataset. What is not clear to me is how the variance between the samples contained in the dataset (e.i. the amount of information)  influences the number of iterations. Let's consider two datasets of the same size, and one contains many samples that are very similar, while the other is composed of samples that are very different and sparse in the input space. How much does the bound of required SGD iterations differ in these two cases? How much the amount of information contained in the datasets and/or the complexity of the considered task influence the amount of dense network pre-training needed for a pruned network to perform well?

The empirical evaluation turns out to be questionable in some aspects. For instance, the authors, for what concerns the 2 layers network, state “Namely, we adopt a ReLU hidden activation and apply a sigmoid output transformation to enable training with binary cross-entropy loss. Experiments are conducted with several different hidden dimensions (i.e., N \in {5K,10K,20K}). We pre-train the two-layer network with an SGD optimizer, the momentum of 0.9, no weight decay, and a batch size of 128, which we found to perform well in multiple different experimental settings. “, therefore the tests are performed using a very specific hyper-parameters setting, and to me, it is not clear how the authors can exclude that this very particular setting did not influence the measured performance.
In appendix C.1 the authors discuss the relationship between the size of the model and optimal learning rate, but the discussion on the selection of the other hyper-parameters (momentum, weights decay, batch size, etc) is missing.
Even the method used to determine the optimality of the lr, and also to assess the model performance is not clear to me. Did the authors use a validation /test set? A similar methodology was used also for the other considered models.

As a final remark, I would like to highlight the fact that the paper is 9 pages long while the appendix is 14 pages long.  In my opinion, a paper that requires more pages for the appendix (that contains relevant information to understand the proposed analysis) than the length of the main paper, is maybe more suitable for a journal than for a conference, which imposes a limit on the number of pages. Since that is just a personal opinion, this last point did not influence my evaluation of the manuscript.
content.summary_of_the_review: Even if the proposed theoretical analysis is interesting in my opinion, the novelty proposed by the authors in this manuscript is below the average for an ICLR paper, in particular, because the authors do not propose a novel solution based on the theoretical observation that they proposed. Moreover, the most interesting part of the analysis is limited to a very specific model.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1242 by Reviewer Fxr2

content.title: Response to reviewer Fxr2
content.comment:
"$\textit{In section 2 the discussed 2 layers network (eq (1)) has a ...the architecture.}$"

This two-layer architecture is a standard neural network architecture used extensively for the theoretical understanding of neural network training; see [1, 2, 3] for a few examples, as well as references to these papers. The architecture is a two layer network with a single output neuron---a learnable transformation is applied to the output of the first layer (after the non-linearity) to yield a single output neuron (i.e., notice (2) contains multiplication by another weight, corresponding to the weight matrix of the second layer). Thus, the network has two weight matrices, one to transform the input into the hidden representation and one to transform the hidden representation into the single output neuron. This architecture is complex enough to deviate from just linear transformations (which would have been the case of matrix factorization). This formulation is very widely used within the current literature, especially when theoretical results are involved, and is definitely non-trivial to handle. Having deeper architectures is always desirable, but, to the best of our knowledge, there is no universal theory that characterizes (in non-asymptotic sense) the convergence behavior of gradient-descent based algorithms in these scenarios (set aside any LTH results on these more complicated scenarios). From a different perspective, there is almost no theory suggesting whether LTH works and why; this paper moves in that direction, along with only a few papers cited in our related work.

"$\textit{For what concerns the structure of the paper … derived.}$"

We can move the related work. We emphasize that this should not be a consideration in evaluating the paper, as it is a matter of taste and there is no perfect solution; e.g., a related work after the introduction often makes no sense, especially when preceding the problem definition.

For Ye et al., we re-derive the entire proof under modified assumptions in Appendix A.1 -- this proof is standalone and does not exclude any needed information from Ye et. al. For the result of  Oymak & Soltanolkotabi et. al, we provide an extensive explanation in Appendix A.2. 

"$\textit{The authors state that the number of SGD … perform well?}$"

The dataset variance (and task complexity) can be implicitly captured within the diameter of the marginal polytope $\mathcal{M}_N$ -- a wider polytope will loosen the upper bound in Theorem 1, implying the guarantees on subnetwork (and dense network) performance degrade as the polytope becomes wider. This makes intuitive sense as networks will have higher loss/lower accuracy on more complex tasks.

The discussion within section 6.1 considers this case exactly, discussing how modifications to constants within our analysis (i.e., by considerations such as task difficulty and variance in the dataset) may impact the performance of the dense/pruned network, but will not impact how much pre-training is required for a sub-network to match dense network performance. In other words, our analysis that derives the bound in pre-training iterations is robust to the factors you mention.

This concern applies to (and challenges) all the literature on overparameterization, which we find unfair to apply as criticism to our paper: the definition of a data sample and contribution of data (through “variance”) to overall training is a big open problem in ML that we do not handle in this work. Putting this differently, the same concern applies to the overparameterized papers that claim overparameterization $N = \mathcal{O}(m^c)$ for some $c$. How variance affects these works is not resolved yet, so we assume that the data come from the same, diverse enough, data distribution. 

"$\textit{The empirical evaluation ... considered models.}$"

Relevant hyperparameters are always tuned using a hold out validation set -- this is shown in appendix C.1. This was done for all models, and we will be more clear about this in the writing.

Momentum and weight decay have minimal impact on network performance. We test several hidden dimensions to prove our findings are robust to network size. The batch size is simply the maximum batch size that fits in our GPUs. We are not sure what the reviewer would like us to do here to avoid “specific” hyperparameter settings -- tuning hyperparameters based on a validation set and presenting the best-performing selection based on a validation set is common practice across the field. We disagree completely that these hyperparameter settings make the empirical analysis questionable. 

"$\textit{As a final … manuscript.}$"

Thank you for your opinion. Yet, we would like to point out that looking at recent ICML/NeurIPS/ICLR submissions, this rule is largely not applicable.

References:

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.01794 

[2] https://francisbach.com/gradient-descent-neural-networks-global-convergence/

[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09545
